content.title: About
content.content: Crackers‑matzo are dry, crunchy flatbreads traditionally made from unfermented wheat flour and water. They are a staple in Jewish cuisine, especially during Passover when leavened bread is prohibited. Matzo has a neutral flavor and can be enjoyed as a snack or used as a base for various toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Matzo is considered the oldest type of bread, dating back to ancient Egypt.
The tradition of eating matzo at Passover originates from the Israelites’ hasty departure from Egypt, when they had no time for dough to rise.
There are several varieties: thin and crisp, as well as thicker, more bread‑like versions.
In some countries matzo is used as a gluten‑free base because it typically contains no leavening agents.
In the United States, “cracker‑style” matzo is sold, which is larger and more flavorful than the traditional thin sheets.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Crackers‑matzo contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Despite their simple appearance, matzo provides slowly released energy thanks to its complex carbs.

items.title: Gluten‑free options
items.content: Matzo made from rice or corn flour is available for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Rich in fiber (when whole‑grain flour is used)
items.content: Some whole‑grain matzo varieties contain dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Matzo does not contain added sugars, making it a good choice for those monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Traditional wheat‑based matzo can trigger allergic reactions in individuals sensitive to gluten.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Because its carbohydrates are quickly absorbed, matzo can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some commercial varieties are salted; people limiting sodium should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Hard texture
items.content: The crisp texture may be difficult for young children or people with chewing difficulties.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Matzo can be eaten plain, spread with cream cheese, hummus, avocado, or used as a base for open‑face sandwiches. In cooking it is often used as a coating for fish or meat and added to salads for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store matzo in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.
